title: Subgroups of Free Groups and Schreier Rewriting

items.title: The labeled Schreier coset graph of a subgroup of a free group
The Schreier coset graph is connected and deterministic
items.strategy: Every coset is reached by reading a reduced word from the base coset, and for each generator there is exactly one outgoing and one inverse incoming labeled edge.

items.title: Schreier transversals and Schreier systems
Rooted spanning trees and Schreier systems correspond
items.strategy: Here a rooted spanning tree means a connected acyclic spanning subgraph of the Schreier graph with the base coset as root. It picks the unique reduced label of the tree path from the base coset to each vertex, and the initial-segment closure is exactly the rooted-tree property.

items.title: Schreier generators in the right-coset convention
Every Schreier generator lies in the subgroup
items.strategy: The chosen representative and the generator land in the same right coset as the reduced representative of their product, so their quotient belongs to the subgroup.

items.title: The Schreier rewriting map
Schreier rewriting is invariant under free reduction
items.strategy: Adjacent inverse letters force consecutive Schreier factors to cancel after tracking the same intermediate coset representative.

items.title: The nontrivial Schreier generators generate the subgroup
items.strategy: Track a subgroup word through successive coset representatives and telescope the resulting Schreier factors; the final representative returns to the base coset.

items.title: Tree Schreier generators are freely independent
items.strategy: A nontrivial reduced product of tree generators determines a non-backtracking closed path using an edge outside the spanning tree, contradicting tree normal form.

items.title: Under the stated choice boundary, every subgroup of a free group is free with its nontrivial Schreier generators as a basis
items.strategy: The Schreier generating lemma gives generation, the tree lemma gives free independence, and the statement separates the finite and countable Schreier-system clauses from the arbitrary-rank formulation, which records its Axiom-of-Choice cost explicitly.

items.title: The Schreier index-rank formula
items.strategy: For a finite-index subgroup, count the non-tree edges in a Schreier graph spanning tree and identify that count with the size of an explicit free basis.

items.title: A free group of rank at least two has subgroups of every finite rank
items.strategy: Choose two basis elements to obtain a rank-two free subgroup, then apply the index-rank formula to finite-index subgroups of that rank-two subgroup.

items.title: The Reidemeister-Schreier presentation theorem
items.strategy: Lift the subgroup to the free group on the presentation generators, use a Schreier transversal there, and rewrite conjugates of defining relators into Schreier generators.

items.title: Reidemeister-Schreier relators are independent of word representatives
items.strategy: Replacing a relator by a freely equivalent word changes its rewrite only by cancellations already controlled by Schreier rewriting invariance, and normal closure absorbs the conjugacy choices.

items.title: Finite-index subgroups of finitely presented groups are finitely presented
items.strategy: For a finite-index subgroup, a Schreier transversal and the defining-relator set are both finite, so the Reidemeister-Schreier presentation has finitely many generators and relators.

items.title: Every finitely generated subgroup of a finite-rank free group is a free factor of a finite-index subgroup
items.strategy: Start from the finite core graph of the subgroup, attach a path for a separating word, fold, and complete to a regular finite covering graph; the spanning-tree basis then splits off the original subgroup as a free factor.

items.title: FALSE: every subgroup of a finitely generated free group is finitely generated
items.strategy: Refute with an infinite-index subgroup of a rank-two free group whose Schreier basis is infinite.

items.title: FALSE: the raw Schreier generators are always a free basis
items.strategy: Refute by exhibiting a transversal that is not a Schreier system or that leaves trivial generators in place, so the resulting family is not the reduced basis guaranteed by the theorem.

items.title: FALSE: a finite-index d subgroup of a rank n free group has rank dn
items.strategy: Apply the exact Schreier index-rank formula and compare it with dn on the simplest nontrivial examples.

items.title: FALSE: the Reidemeister-Schreier presentation needs no choice of transversal
items.strategy: Different transversals produce different Schreier generators and rewritten relators even though the resulting presented subgroup is isomorphic.

title: Subgroups of Free Groups and Schreier Rewriting — Examples

items.title: An index-two subgroup of a rank-two free group has rank three
items.strategy: Write the two cosets, choose a Schreier system, list the nontrivial generators, and verify the rank with the Schreier formula.

items.title: The kernel of an exponent-sum map in a free group
items.strategy: Use a Schreier transversal for the kernel of the map to Z, compute the resulting generators, and see directly why the basis is infinite.

items.title: A Schreier coset graph and its spanning-tree basis
items.strategy: Draw the labeled coset graph, choose a rooted spanning tree, and read off the explicit Schreier basis from the non-tree edges.

items.title: A Reidemeister-Schreier presentation for a surface subgroup
items.strategy: Choose a transversal in the ambient presentation, rewrite the conjugated relators, and simplify the resulting presentation to the expected surface form.

items.title: A rank-two free group contains an infinite-rank subgroup
items.strategy: Compute the Schreier basis of a natural infinite-index subgroup and exhibit infinitely many distinct nontrivial Schreier generators.

items.title: Marshall Hall's theorem produces a separating finite-index overgroup
items.strategy: Adjoin a path for a word outside the subgroup, complete the folded graph to a finite covering, and read off the free-factor splitting.

items.title: An arbitrary transversal need not give the reduced Schreier basis
items.strategy: Pick coset representatives that fail the Schreier initial-segment condition and show that the resulting generator list contains redundancy or trivial elements.

items.title: Means on bounded functions on a group
Left translation on bounded functions
Left-invariant means and amenable groups
Left and right amenability agree by inversion
items.strategy: Precompose bounded functions with inversion to transport a left-invariant mean into a right-invariant one and conversely.

items.title: Finite groups are amenable
items.strategy: Normalized counting on the finite underlying set gives an invariant mean.

items.title: Abelian groups are amenable
items.strategy: Use the directed-union reduction to finitely generated abelian groups and then build an invariant mean from Folner sets, recording the ultrafilter cost explicitly.

items.title: Subgroups and quotients of amenable groups are amenable
items.strategy: Restrict an invariant measure to a subgroup by a transversal argument and push amenability to a quotient through the induced action on cosets.

items.title: Extensions of amenable groups are amenable
items.strategy: Combine invariant means on the normal subgroup and the quotient by averaging first along cosets and then over the quotient.

items.title: Locally finite groups
Directed unions of amenable subgroups are amenable
items.strategy: View the ambient group as the direct limit of the directed system of amenable subgroups and pass invariant finitely additive measures to the limit.

items.title: Solvable groups and locally finite groups are amenable
items.strategy: For solvable groups, induct on derived length using the extension theorem; for locally finite groups, express the group as the directed union of its finite subgroups.

items.title: Folner sets and the Folner condition
Equivalent boundary formulations of the Folner condition
items.strategy: Rewrite symmetric-difference estimates as boundary estimates and compare right and left formulations by inversion.

items.title: The Folner criterion for amenability
items.strategy: Build a mean from Folner sets via an ultrafilter limit, and conversely use finite-dimensional separation to extract almost invariant finite sets from an invariant mean.

items.title: Folner sequences for enumerated groups
Enumerated countable amenable groups admit Folner sequences
items.strategy: Exhaust the group by the finite subsets cut out by the enumeration and choose successive Folner sets with error at most 1/n for the nth finite test set.

items.title: Subexponential growth implies amenability
items.strategy: Use growth balls: if every radius had proportionally large boundary, iterating the boundary growth would force exponential growth.

items.title: Paradoxical decompositions of groups
Paradoxical groups admit no invariant mean
items.strategy: An invariant mean applied to the two translated disjoint decompositions forces 1 to be at least 2.

items.title: A group is amenable if and only if it is not paradoxical
items.strategy: Invoke Tarski's finitely additive measure criterion for paradoxical subsets and specialize it to the left action of the group on itself.

items.title: The free group of rank two is nonamenable
items.strategy: Use either the invariant-mean contradiction from the standard two-piece decomposition or an explicit paradoxical decomposition of reduced words in a free basis.

items.title: Groups containing a rank-two free subgroup are nonamenable
items.strategy: An amenable group has amenable subgroups, so a rank-two free subgroup contradicts the previous theorem.

items.title: Amenability is a quasi-isometry invariant for finitely generated groups
items.strategy: Transfer Folner sets across a quasi-isometry using bounded distortion of boundaries and bounded geometry of Cayley graphs.

items.title: There exist nonamenable groups without nonabelian free subgroups
FALSE: amenable means finite
items.strategy: Refute with infinite abelian groups such as Z.

items.title: FALSE: every nonamenable group contains a rank-two free subgroup
items.strategy: Refute by citing standard nonamenable counterexamples without nonabelian free subgroups.

items.title: FALSE: one finite Folner set proves amenability
items.strategy: The criterion quantifies over every finite test set and every error tolerance, not one accidental almost-invariant finite subset.

items.title: FALSE: every uncountable amenable group has a Folner sequence
items.strategy: The sequence formulation needs a countable indexing of the finite tests; in general one uses Folner nets or the finite-test property itself.

items.title: FALSE: a paradoxical decomposition is just an abstract partition without prescribed translates
items.strategy: The translating group elements are load-bearing: without them the decomposition no longer encodes nonamenability.

title: Amenable Groups and Folner Criteria — Examples

items.title: Intervals in Z are Folner sets
items.strategy: Compute the boundary of symmetric intervals explicitly for a fixed finite generating set and let the interval radius grow.

items.title: Boxes in Z^n are Folner sets
items.strategy: Count the boundary layers of cubes in the standard basis and compare them with the total number of lattice points.

items.title: Finite groups and locally finite groups are amenable
items.strategy: Apply normalized counting in the finite case and the directed-union corollary in the locally finite case.

items.title: The standard lamplighter group is amenable
items.strategy: Describe the lamplighter group as a semidirect product of a locally finite base by Z and apply the extension theorem.

items.title: Boundary expansion in the free group
items.strategy: Show that every finite set of reduced words in a free basis acquires a uniformly positive boundary proportion under multiplication by generators.

items.title: A paradoxical decomposition of a free group of rank two
items.strategy: Partition reduced words by initial letter and write the group as two disjoint translated copies.

items.title: Amenability does not imply subexponential growth
items.strategy: Use the lamplighter group as an amenable group with exponential growth.
